chapterTitle: Understanding Augmented Reality (AR) and Virtual Reality (VR)
aiGenerationNote: Create a 12-minute animated explainer video. Start with clear visual definitions of AR, VR, and MR using distinct graphical representations (e.g., VR: person fully inside a digital world; AR: digital overlay on real world; MR: digital objects interacting with real world). Showcase diverse real-world examples for each, such as a surgeon using AR overlays, a student on a VR field trip, or an architect reviewing a 3D model in MR. Include a segment demonstrating common AR and VR hardware (smartphone AR, standalone VR headset, PC-tethered VR, AR glasses). Emphasize common mistakes like confusing the terms or neglecting user comfort, with visual cues like a dizzy user in VR. screens.title: Understanding AR and VR
screens.narratorSegment: Welcome. In this short orientation you'll build a mental map of augmented reality and virtual reality before writing a single line of Unity code. AR augments your view of the real world with digital content, while VR replaces your surroundings with a simulated environment. Both approaches share the goal of changing perception, but each raises different design, hardware, and safety trade-offs. During this lesson you will learn precise definitions, identify the core technical building blocks like stereoscopic displays, head tracking, and spatial mapping, and see concrete examples such as surgical VR training and AR assisted maintenance. You will also learn the difference between AR and the deeper integration called mixed reality, and why device choice—smartphone, standalone headset, or AR glasses—shapes what is possible. Finally, we'll point out common beginner mistakes, like confusing AR with MR or neglecting user comfort in VR, and provide a short activity so you can connect examples to a specific industry. By the end of this chapter you will be able to name the right technology for a given problem and explain basic hardware constraints that influence design. Ask yourself: which problems in your area require full immersion and which benefit from augmentation?

Understanding AR & VR
What they are, how they differ, and real-world uses that matter.
Interactive 16:9 Masterclass

Orientation
Why this chapter matters

Immersive systems change how people sense and act. Choosing the correct approach—augmenting or fully immersing—affects interaction design, safety, and hardware constraints. This chapter gives you the vocabulary and practical examples to choose wisely.

AR, VR, MR
Hardware
Headsets, smartphones, glasses
Use cases
Healthcare, retail, education

Full immersion, simulated worlds
Augmented Reality

Digital and physical interacting

Hardware
Smartphones, standalone headsets, AR glasses and their constraints.
Applications
Healthcare, education, retail, manufacturing, tourism.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: By the end of this chapter you will confidently differentiate AR, VR, and MR with concrete examples and explain why the distinction matters for design and hardware choices. You will identify the core components that make immersive experiences work: displays, tracking, and spatial understanding. You will recognize the common hardware platforms—smartphones and tablets for AR, standalone and PC-tethered headsets for VR, and specialized glasses for mixed reality—and understand how each platform constrains interaction and fidelity. Finally, you will be able to discuss several cross-industry applications and connect them to appropriate hardware and design priorities. For example, you will explain why surgical VR training benefits from high-fidelity, PC-tethered headsets, while AR remote assistance is effective on tablets or smart glasses. Each objective includes a small visual mnemonic to anchor the idea and a verified competency milestone so you know when you are ready to move on.

screens.title: What is Virtual Reality (VR)?
screens.narratorSegment: Virtual Reality is a simulated experience that replaces your physical surroundings with a digital environment. The defining technical traits include stereoscopic displays that present slightly different images to each eye, head tracking that updates the view as you look around, and often hand-held controllers that let you interact with objects. Together, these elements attempt to create a sense of presence—the psychological feeling of 'being there'. A concrete example from the chapter is a surgical training simulation where a trainee enters a virtual operating room and practices procedures in a risk-free setting using a PC-tethered headset for high-fidelity visuals. A common misconception is that VR is only for gaming; in fact, VR's full immersion makes it valuable for training, therapy, design reviews, and remote collaboration. Another pitfall is assuming presence is automatic: poor frame rates, incorrect interpupillary distance settings, or mismatched motion cues will break immersion and can cause motion sickness. Key design implications are hardware choice and user comfort: PC-tethered headsets can deliver higher graphic fidelity but require more setup, while standalone headsets trade some fidelity for ease of use. Takeaway: VR replaces perception, and achieving convincing presence requires coordinated hardware and careful performance tuning. Consider: which tasks truly need full immersion, and which can be solved with augmentation instead?

keyIdea.title: VR in one sentence
keyIdea.text: VR fully replaces the user's view with a simulated environment; presence depends on synchronized displays and tracking.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.1 › What is Virtual Reality (VR)?
Definition
Virtual Reality

A fully simulated environment presented via headsets using stereoscopic imagery and head tracking. Designed to replace the user's surroundings and create presence.

Core traits
  • Stereoscopic 3D displays for depth.
  • Head tracking for natural viewpoint changes.
  • Controllers or hand input for interaction.
Common mistake
Assuming VR is only gaming or that presence happens without tuning frame rates and IPD. Performance and comfort are essential design constraints.
Concrete example
Surgical training in VR

Trainees enter a virtual operating room using a PC-tethered headset, manipulate instruments, and receive performance feedback without risking patients.

Key Takeaway
Key Takeaway

VR requires coordinated hardware and software to create presence. Prioritize performance and comfort when designing immersive experiences.

screens.title: What is Augmented Reality (AR)?
screens.narratorSegment: Augmented Reality augments the user's view of the real world by overlaying digital content that complements or enhances physical surroundings. This can be as simple as a heads-up text label or as complex as a 3D model that appears anchored to a table in your room. Common consumer AR runs on smartphones and tablets using their cameras to capture the environment and place content on top. Specialized AR glasses project imagery into your field of view and allow hands-free use. A clear example from the chapter is a retail 'try-before-you-buy' app that places a 3D sofa model in a customer's living room so they can judge fit and style through their phone. A common misconception is to assume AR simply means decorative overlays; true AR can and should respect spatial relationships—correct scale, occlusion, and lighting—otherwise the illusion breaks and the user's trust drops. Design implications include understanding the limitations of camera tracking and the need to balance fidelity with battery life and C P U constraints on mobile devices. Takeaway: AR keeps you grounded in the real world while adding useful context. Ask yourself: what information improves a user's real-world decision without blocking their view?

keyIdea.title: AR in one sentence

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.1 › What is AR?
Definition
Augmented Reality

An interactive experience where digital objects are overlaid onto your view of the world, often using device cameras or transparent optics, preserving awareness of surroundings.

Forms
  • 2D overlays and filters.
  • 3D models anchored to surfaces.
  • Wearable visual overlays via glasses.
Design note
Maintain scale, occlusion, and lighting to make augmentations believable; otherwise users may distrust the experience.
Concrete example
Try-before-you-buy retail AR

A shopper points a phone at their living room and sees a 3D sofa placed to scale. This reduces returns and increases buyer confidence by showing products in context.

Key Takeaway
Key Takeaway

AR augments awareness. Choose AR when the physical context matters and when overlays improve a real-world task.

screens.title: What is Mixed Reality (MR)?
screens.narratorSegment: Mixed Reality sits between AR and VR and emphasizes deeper integration between digital and physical elements. MR experiences not only overlay digital objects but also make them behave as if they share the same space: objects occlude behind furniture, cast shadows consistent with scene lighting, and respond to spatial constraints. This requires advanced spatial mapping and environment understanding so the system knows where floors, walls, and obstacles are. A practical illustration is an MR device that lets a virtual character walk behind a real sofa and have its shadow appear on the floor—this level of integration supports natural, intuitive interactions. A frequent misconception is that MR is a separate market; instead it is better viewed as a higher-fidelity class of AR that depends on richer sensors and compute. Devices like the HoloLens are often labeled MR because they include environmental scanning and occlusion support. For design, MR raises the bar for testing in real spaces and demands more robust spatial mapping algorithms. Takeaway: MR unlocks richer interactions by treating digital objects as first-class participants in the real world. Consider whether your project needs full occlusion, shadows, and accurate spatial response before committing to MR-level hardware and development effort.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.1 › What is Mixed Reality (MR)?
Definition
Mixed Reality

MR blends physical and virtual elements so they interact in real time, respecting occlusion, scale, and lighting. It typically relies on spatial mapping to integrate content convincingly into the environment.

Spatial mapping
Scanning the environment to locate surfaces and obstacles for correct placement and occlusion.
Occlusion & shadows
Digital objects hide behind real objects and cast realistic shadows to increase believability.
Interaction fidelity
MR supports more natural interactions because digital objects behave like physical ones in the same space.
Concrete example
Architectural review with occlusion

An architect places a 3D model in a real room; team members can walk around and see virtual features correctly occlude and cast shadows, enabling better spatial judgment.

screens.title: Immersion vs Presence
screens.narratorSegment: Immersion and presence are related but distinct concepts. Immersion refers to the objective qualities of a system—the hardware and software features such as stereoscopic displays, field of view, and tracking fidelity. Presence is the subjective psychological response: the user’s feeling of actually existing within the virtual scene. You can have high immersion but low presence if implementation details are wrong; for example, perfect visuals paired with input lag or mismatched motion cues will break presence. A concrete contrast: a headset offering wide field of view and high resolution provides immersion potential, but poor frame rates or badly tuned interpupillary distance will reduce presence and can create discomfort. A common misconception is to treat presence as automatic; designers must manage latency, consistent motion cues, and comfortable locomotion to sustain presence. Practically, this means prioritizing stable frame rates, correct tracking, and respecting user comfort settings. Takeaway: design decisions that improve immersion—like better displays—only deliver presence when paired with careful usability and performance tuning. Consider: which platform constraints in your target device threaten presence, and how will you address them? Immersion vs Presence means immersion is system capability; presence is the user's psychological response. both must be managed together for convincing experiences.. In practical terms, how technical systems create psychological 'being there'. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.1 › Immersion vs Presence
Immersion
System qualities that enable convincing worlds
  • Stereoscopic displays and wide field of view.
  • High and stable frame rates.
  • Accurate head and controller tracking.
Misconception
High-resolution graphics alone guarantee presence. They do not if tracking or latency are poor.
Presence
The user's feeling of being there

Presence arises when sensory cues, interactivity, and system performance align. It is measured by users' subjective sense of engagement and realism.

Key Takeaway

Presence requires both capable hardware and careful UX to avoid discomfort and preserve realism.

screens.title: VR Hardware: Standalone vs PC-Tethered
screens.narratorSegment: VR headsets come in two common classes: standalone and PC-tethered. Standalone headsets include their own processors and run without a separate computer, which makes them convenient, portable, and easier to deploy. This convenience often comes at the cost of raw graphics fidelity and complex physics simulations. PC-tethered headsets are connected to a powerful computer and can render higher-resolution scenes, offer better tracking in some setups, and support demanding simulations like surgical training or high-end design reviews. A concrete example: a surgical training simulation benefits from a PC-tethered headset to achieve finer visual detail and accurate instrument physics. A common beginner error is choosing a standalone headset solely for convenience without accounting for the performance requirements of the experience. Conversely, choosing a PC-tethered setup when the use case calls for portability can hinder real-world deployment. When designing, ask whether fidelity or accessibility matters more for your target users. Key takeaway: match the hardware class to the experience goals and constraints, and document expected trade-offs early in your project plan. Module 1 › Chapter 1.1 › VR Hardware
Comparison
Standalone vs PC-tethered
Standalone
Self-contained, portable, easier to deploy but lower max fidelity and compute for complex simulations.
PC-tethered
Requires a connected computer, supports higher fidelity rendering, physics, and precision—better for high-stakes training.
Design question
Does your experience require top visual fidelity and physics accuracy, or portability and ease of use in the real world?
Concrete example
Surgical training uses PC-tethered systems

High-resolution visuals and realistic instrument behavior often need the extra compute of a PC to deliver valid training outcomes.

Key Takeaway
Key Takeaway

Choose hardware based on fidelity needs and deployment constraints, not just availability.

screens.title: AR Hardware: Smartphones, Tablets, and Glasses
screens.narratorSegment: AR experiences are commonly deployed on smartphones and tablets because these devices already include cameras, displays, and sufficient sensors for many augmentation tasks. This makes AR widely accessible and easy to distribute via apps. The chapter highlights smartphone AR examples like furniture visualization and museum guides. Specialized AR glasses, such as devices that project imagery directly into your field of view, offer hands-free operation and better integration with the environment but are currently less ubiquitous and still evolving. A concrete example in the chapter is AR remote assistance where an on-site technician uses smart glasses to share their view while an expert overlays instructions. A typical beginner mistake is assuming glasses will behave exactly like phone AR; glasses often have different field of view, device compute, and interaction models. Design implications include planning for the lowest common denominator: if you target phones, optimize for battery, C P U constraints, and camera tracking variability. If you target glasses, design for hands-free interaction and persistent overlays. Takeaway: match interaction and deployment needs to the right AR hardware class and test in representative real spaces.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.1 › AR Hardware
Platforms
Smartphones & Tablets

Most AR experiences run on phone cameras and are widely accessible. They are suitable for visual overlays and spatial placement but face battery and tracking variability.

Design note
Optimize for varying lighting, camera quality, and performance across devices when targeting phones and tablets.
Platforms
AR Glasses

Glasses enable hands-free workflows and persistent overlays, useful for remote assistance and industrial maintenance, though they require different interaction models and testing approaches.

Concrete example
AR remote assistance with glasses—an expert annotates the technician's real-time view to guide repairs.

screens.title: Core Components of AR/VR Systems
screens.narratorSegment: Immersive systems rely on several core components that work together to produce believable experiences. Displays deliver imagery—VR headsets use stereoscopic displays while AR typically overlays rendered content onto camera or optical feeds. Tracking systems, including head and controller tracking, update the virtual camera as users move their head or hands. Spatial mapping senses the environment to identify floors and surfaces for placing or occluding digital objects; this is essential for MR. Input devices such as controllers, hand tracking, or gaze-based selection let users interact with virtual content. A concrete example: a maintenance AR system uses a tablet camera for scene understanding, spatial mapping to anchor instructions to specific machine parts, and a remote expert's annotations that appear aligned with the physical components. A common misconception is that components are interchangeable; in practice, the choice of display dictates available input and mapping strategies. For design, document required component fidelity early—what level of tracking accuracy or spatial mapping do you need—and test with representative hardware. Takeaway: successful experiences are the result of thoughtful integration across displays, tracking, spatial mapping, and input, not any single component in isolation.

keyIdea.text: Displays, tracking, mapping, and input must be specified and tested together to produce convincing AR/VR experiences.

Components
Displays
Stereoscopic headsets for VR; camera feeds or transparent optics for AR.
Tracking
Head and controller tracking to update viewpoint and interaction in real time.
Spatial mapping
Environment scanning to place and occlude digital objects accurately for AR and MR.
Input
Controllers, hand tracking, and gaze-based input provide interactivity with virtual elements.
Concrete scenario
Tablet-based AR for field service

A tablet camera captures the machine, spatial mapping anchors step-by-step instructions to components, and the technician taps onscreen markers to advance the procedure while a remote expert annotates the live view.

Key Takeaway

screens.title: AR and VR Use Cases Across Industries
screens.narratorSegment: AR and VR find useful applications across healthcare, education, retail, manufacturing, and tourism, each leveraging different facets of immersion and augmentation. In healthcare, VR supports surgical training and therapy while AR can overlay patient data during surgery. In education, VR enables virtual field trips that transport students to distant places, and AR turns textbooks into interactive experiences that sit alongside the learner’s view. Retail uses AR for try-before-you-buy visualizations, allowing customers to place products in their homes to reduce uncertainty. Manufacturing and engineering use AR for maintenance guides and assembly instructions, while VR supports design reviews and prototyping in a controlled digital space. A common misconception is to treat these as novelty; instead, each use case solves a specific operational problem—training without risk, reducing returns, speeding repairs, or scaling access to distant experiences. When mapping use cases to technology, identify the problem you solve first, then choose AR, VR, or MR based on whether the user needs to stay in the real world or be fully immersed. Takeaway: match the right technology to the problem and explain the hardware choices that follow.

screens.title: Designing for Comfort and Safety
screens.narratorSegment: User comfort and safety must be primary concerns in AR/VR design. In VR, headsets block the user's view of the real environment, so ensuring a clear play space and providing boundary systems like a virtual guardian or chaperone is essential to prevent collisions. Motion sickness is commonly caused by low or unstable frame rates, mismatched motion cues, or sudden camera movement that the user did not initiate. Designers should prioritize stable performance, provide comfortable locomotion options, and allow adjustable settings like interpupillary distance and motion sensitivity. In AR, though users retain awareness of their surroundings, distractions and occlusion of important real-world cues can still lead to accidents; remind users to remain aware of obstacles when walking with a device. A common mistake is ignoring safety until late in development; instead, include safety checks and comfort testing on early prototypes. Test experiences in representative physical spaces, try slow locomotion options, and provide clear user guidance about required play space. Takeaway: safety and comfort are not extras — they enable longer sessions and better learning outcomes. Ask: how will you test comfort and what safeguards will you provide for users in real spaces?

Best Practices
Clear play space
Use virtual boundaries and instruct users to remove hazards before starting VR sessions.
Performance stability
Prioritize consistent frame rates and avoid sudden camera movements to reduce motion sickness.
Adjustable comfort options
Provide locomotion alternatives and adjustable settings for users sensitive to motion.
Concrete checklist

  • Include a guardian or boundary system for VR.

Common mistake
Neglecting safety testing until late—this increases risk and can force costly redesigns.

Virtual Reality (VR)
A simulated experience that replaces the user's perception of the real world.
Augmented Reality (AR)
Digital information overlaid on the real world, preserving awareness of surroundings.

screens.narratorSegment: These operational terms help you design responsibly. Immersion and presence are distinct: immersion is the technical capability while presence is the user's psychological response. fullNarratorScript:
Welcome. In this short orientation you'll build a mental map of augmented reality and virtual reality before writing a single line of Unity code. AR augments your view of the real world with digital content, while VR replaces your surroundings with a simulated environment. Both approaches share the goal of changing perception, but each raises different design, hardware, and safety trade-offs. During this lesson you will learn precise definitions, identify the core technical building blocks like stereoscopic displays, head tracking, and spatial mapping, and see concrete examples such as surgical VR training and AR assisted maintenance. You will also learn the difference between AR and the deeper integration called mixed reality, and why device choice—smartphone, standalone headset, or AR glasses—shapes what is possible. Finally, we'll point out common beginner mistakes, like confusing AR with MR or neglecting user comfort in VR, and provide a short activity so you can connect examples to a specific industry. By the end of this chapter you will be able to name the right technology for a given problem and explain basic hardware constraints that influence design. Ask yourself: which problems in your area require full immersion and which benefit from augmentation?

By the end of this chapter you will confidently differentiate AR, VR, and MR with concrete examples and explain why the distinction matters for design and hardware choices. You will identify the core components that make immersive experiences work: displays, tracking, and spatial understanding. You will recognize the common hardware platforms—smartphones and tablets for AR, standalone and PC-tethered headsets for VR, and specialized glasses for mixed reality—and understand how each platform constrains interaction and fidelity. Finally, you will be able to discuss several cross-industry applications and connect them to appropriate hardware and design priorities. For example, you will explain why surgical VR training benefits from high-fidelity, PC-tethered headsets, while AR remote assistance is effective on tablets or smart glasses. Each objective includes a small visual mnemonic to anchor the idea and a verified competency milestone so you know when you are ready to move on.

This mini-bar helps you track cognitive growth as you work through the chapter. First you will learn names and simple distinctions—what AR, VR, and MR mean. Next you will understand the building blocks: why stereoscopic images, head tracking, and spatial mapping matter. Then you will apply that knowledge to choose hardware and sketch basic interaction flows for a use case. Finally you will master the judgment to map real problems to the right technology and explain trade-offs. Each step builds on the previous. For example, simply naming a headset is not enough; you must understand how a standalone headset's self-contained processing limits graphics fidelity compared with a PC-tethered system. That understanding is what lets you make practical design decisions. Keep this progression in mind while you explore examples and the hands-on activity.

Virtual Reality is a simulated experience that replaces your physical surroundings with a digital environment. The defining technical traits include stereoscopic displays that present slightly different images to each eye, head tracking that updates the view as you look around, and often hand-held controllers that let you interact with objects. Together, these elements attempt to create a sense of presence—the psychological feeling of 'being there'. A concrete example from the chapter is a surgical training simulation where a trainee enters a virtual operating room and practices procedures in a risk-free setting using a PC-tethered headset for high-fidelity visuals. A common misconception is that VR is only for gaming; in fact, VR's full immersion makes it valuable for training, therapy, design reviews, and remote collaboration. Another pitfall is assuming presence is automatic: poor frame rates, incorrect interpupillary distance settings, or mismatched motion cues will break immersion and can cause motion sickness. Key design implications are hardware choice and user comfort: PC-tethered headsets can deliver higher graphic fidelity but require more setup, while standalone headsets trade some fidelity for ease of use. Takeaway: VR replaces perception, and achieving convincing presence requires coordinated hardware and careful performance tuning. Consider: which tasks truly need full immersion, and which can be solved with augmentation instead?

Augmented Reality augments the user's view of the real world by overlaying digital content that complements or enhances physical surroundings. This can be as simple as a heads-up text label or as complex as a 3D model that appears anchored to a table in your room. Common consumer AR runs on smartphones and tablets using their cameras to capture the environment and place content on top. Specialized AR glasses project imagery into your field of view and allow hands-free use. A clear example from the chapter is a retail 'try-before-you-buy' app that places a 3D sofa model in a customer's living room so they can judge fit and style through their phone. A common misconception is to assume AR simply means decorative overlays; true AR can and should respect spatial relationships—correct scale, occlusion, and lighting—otherwise the illusion breaks and the user's trust drops. Design implications include understanding the limitations of camera tracking and the need to balance fidelity with battery life and C P U constraints on mobile devices. Takeaway: AR keeps you grounded in the real world while adding useful context. Ask yourself: what information improves a user's real-world decision without blocking their view?

Mixed Reality sits between AR and VR and emphasizes deeper integration between digital and physical elements. MR experiences not only overlay digital objects but also make them behave as if they share the same space: objects occlude behind furniture, cast shadows consistent with scene lighting, and respond to spatial constraints. This requires advanced spatial mapping and environment understanding so the system knows where floors, walls, and obstacles are. A practical illustration is an MR device that lets a virtual character walk behind a real sofa and have its shadow appear on the floor—this level of integration supports natural, intuitive interactions. A frequent misconception is that MR is a separate market; instead it is better viewed as a higher-fidelity class of AR that depends on richer sensors and compute. Devices like the HoloLens are often labeled MR because they include environmental scanning and occlusion support. For design, MR raises the bar for testing in real spaces and demands more robust spatial mapping algorithms. Takeaway: MR unlocks richer interactions by treating digital objects as first-class participants in the real world. Consider whether your project needs full occlusion, shadows, and accurate spatial response before committing to MR-level hardware and development effort.

Immersion and presence are related but distinct concepts. Immersion refers to the objective qualities of a system—the hardware and software features such as stereoscopic displays, field of view, and tracking fidelity. Presence is the subjective psychological response: the user’s feeling of actually existing within the virtual scene. You can have high immersion but low presence if implementation details are wrong; for example, perfect visuals paired with input lag or mismatched motion cues will break presence. A concrete contrast: a headset offering wide field of view and high resolution provides immersion potential, but poor frame rates or badly tuned interpupillary distance will reduce presence and can create discomfort. A common misconception is to treat presence as automatic; designers must manage latency, consistent motion cues, and comfortable locomotion to sustain presence. Practically, this means prioritizing stable frame rates, correct tracking, and respecting user comfort settings. Takeaway: design decisions that improve immersion—like better displays—only deliver presence when paired with careful usability and performance tuning. Consider: which platform constraints in your target device threaten presence, and how will you address them? Immersion vs Presence means immersion is system capability; presence is the user's psychological response. both must be managed together for convincing experiences.. In practical terms, how technical systems create psychological 'being there'. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

VR headsets come in two common classes: standalone and PC-tethered. Standalone headsets include their own processors and run without a separate computer, which makes them convenient, portable, and easier to deploy. This convenience often comes at the cost of raw graphics fidelity and complex physics simulations. PC-tethered headsets are connected to a powerful computer and can render higher-resolution scenes, offer better tracking in some setups, and support demanding simulations like surgical training or high-end design reviews. A concrete example: a surgical training simulation benefits from a PC-tethered headset to achieve finer visual detail and accurate instrument physics. A common beginner error is choosing a standalone headset solely for convenience without accounting for the performance requirements of the experience. Conversely, choosing a PC-tethered setup when the use case calls for portability can hinder real-world deployment. When designing, ask whether fidelity or accessibility matters more for your target users. Key takeaway: match the hardware class to the experience goals and constraints, and document expected trade-offs early in your project plan. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

AR experiences are commonly deployed on smartphones and tablets because these devices already include cameras, displays, and sufficient sensors for many augmentation tasks. This makes AR widely accessible and easy to distribute via apps. The chapter highlights smartphone AR examples like furniture visualization and museum guides. Specialized AR glasses, such as devices that project imagery directly into your field of view, offer hands-free operation and better integration with the environment but are currently less ubiquitous and still evolving. A concrete example in the chapter is AR remote assistance where an on-site technician uses smart glasses to share their view while an expert overlays instructions. A typical beginner mistake is assuming glasses will behave exactly like phone AR; glasses often have different field of view, device compute, and interaction models. Design implications include planning for the lowest common denominator: if you target phones, optimize for battery, C P U constraints, and camera tracking variability. If you target glasses, design for hands-free interaction and persistent overlays. Takeaway: match interaction and deployment needs to the right AR hardware class and test in representative real spaces.

Immersive systems rely on several core components that work together to produce believable experiences. Displays deliver imagery—VR headsets use stereoscopic displays while AR typically overlays rendered content onto camera or optical feeds. Tracking systems, including head and controller tracking, update the virtual camera as users move their head or hands. Spatial mapping senses the environment to identify floors and surfaces for placing or occluding digital objects; this is essential for MR. Input devices such as controllers, hand tracking, or gaze-based selection let users interact with virtual content. A concrete example: a maintenance AR system uses a tablet camera for scene understanding, spatial mapping to anchor instructions to specific machine parts, and a remote expert's annotations that appear aligned with the physical components. A common misconception is that components are interchangeable; in practice, the choice of display dictates available input and mapping strategies. For design, document required component fidelity early—what level of tracking accuracy or spatial mapping do you need—and test with representative hardware. Takeaway: successful experiences are the result of thoughtful integration across displays, tracking, spatial mapping, and input, not any single component in isolation.
